EPIC announces AmeriCorps VISTA Award

2026-08-14

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Empowering Pacific Island Communities, Inc. (EPIC) is pleased to announce that its AmeriCorps VISTA application for federal assistance has been approved, authorizing three AmeriCorps VISTA members to strengthen organizational and community capacity and expand economic opportunity for low-income individuals and families throughout American Samoa.

The approved project, Empowering Pacific Island Communities, will operate from August 23, 2026 through August 7, 2027 under Project Grant #26VSIAS001.The initiative supports EPIC’s Comprehensive Economic Self- Sufficiency Model by strengthening workforce development, education, caregiver workforce development, community partnerships, outreach, data systems, and long-term organizational sustainability.

EPIC is also pleased to announce the selection of Gina Coffin as its Community Outreach & Public Communication VISTA. Gina brings a background in Health Communications and holds a Bachelor’s degree in Health from New Mexico Highlands University. She will strengthen EPIC’s outreach and communication systems, develop culturally responsive awareness materials and campaigns, enhance social media and stakeholder communications, and expand awareness of workforce, education, caregiver training, and economic self- sufficiency opportunities throughout American Samoa.

Butler once again rejected by House for ASEDA board

2026-08-13

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The House of Representatives has once more declined to confirm Brett Butler to the Board of Directors of the American Samoa Economic Development Authority (ASEDA), marking the second unsuccessful vote on his appointment in just over a year.

In July of last year, Butler’s nomination fell short when only ten representatives voted in support while seven opposed. House rules require eleven votes for confirmation, leaving Butler one vote shy.

A motion for reconsideration, introduced by Rep. Luaitaua Gene Pan, was approved the same day. The reconsideration vote was held Tuesday, but the outcome remained unchanged — this time, with ten votes against confirmation and eight votes in support.

Butler’s nomination has drawn attention largely because of his extensive background in both the private sector and government finance.

He is a veteran executive with more than 30 years of experience in operations and financial management. Butler was the first local General Manager of StarKist Samoa, serving nine years in the Territory’s largest private‑sector employer. He later joined Bumble Bee Foods, rising through several senior leadership roles, including Vice President of Loining Operations, Vice President & General Manager of the Santa Fe Springs branch, and Vice President of Finance Operations.

After returning to American Samoa, Butler served as Executive Advisor for Finance in the Governor’s Office before being appointed Acting Treasurer in September 2025. His tenure included efforts to modernize ASG’s outdated financial systems, strengthen internal controls, and improve fiscal transparency.

During his confirmation hearing for his appointment as Government Treasurer, legislators described him as a model of local leadership returning home to serve the Territory. Senate Budget Chairman Utu Sila Poasa highlighted Butler’s career trajectory as an example of the kind of expertise American Samoa needs in its financial institutions.

He was unanimously approved by the Senate but fell short of confirmation in the House, a pattern that has been repeated in his nomination to ASEDA Board of Directors.

Supporters had described him as a seasoned executive bringing global industry experience back to the Territory. His nomination to ASEDA was seen as aligning with the authority’s mission of overseeing major financing mechanisms for development projects.

The Senate had previously endorsed Butler’s appointment in March of last year with a unanimous 17 – 0 vote, signaling strong support in the upper chamber. However, ASEDA board appointments require concurrence from both chambers, and the House’s repeated rejection effectively blocks Butler from taking the seat.

With the House denying confirmation for a second time, the administration may submit a new nominee for the ASEDA board seat, attempt another reconsideration if procedurally allowed, or withdraw the nomination entirely.

ASEDA plays a central role in financing major infrastructure and development initiatives, making board appointments closely watched within government and business circles.

Raised crosswalks draw widespread motorists and lawmakers complaints

2026-08-12

DPW says they are part of federally funded Islandwide Safety Project

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Senators were informed last Friday that the so‑called “speed bumps,” that are drawing widespread complaints from motorists and lawmakers, are not speed bumps at all, but raised crosswalks — a federally funded safety feature installed as part of the Islandwide Safety Project.

The clarification came during a Senate Public Works Committee hearing, where Deputy Director of Public Works Falava‘i Ta‘ase explained that the raised crosswalks recently constructed in front of Manumalo Academy, SPICC, and Matafao Elementary School were approved and funded by the U.S. Federal Highway Administration (FHWA).

Ta‘ase told senators that FHWA’s push for raised crosswalks is based on national research. A 2016 nationwide study documented a significant rise in pedestrian‑related traffic accidents occurring at traditional painted crosswalks. A follow‑up study in 2023 found a 45% reduction in crosswalk‑related accidents in areas where raised crosswalks were installed.

He said FHWA formally advised Public Works in 2023 to begin evaluating raised crosswalks for American Samoa. The department initially held back, conducting its own assessment of local traffic patterns and crash data. But with traffic accidents increasing last year and again this year, Public Works determined it was time to begin installing raised crosswalks to improve pedestrian safety and reduce vehicle speeds in high‑risk zones.

Ta‘ase explained that the federal criteria for raised crosswalk placement include a speed limit that must be under 30 mph, the traffic volume must be at least 9,000 vehicles, and the roadway must have no more than three lanes.

He said the locations selected so far meet these requirements, particularly school zones where pedestrian traffic is heavy, and vehicle speeds are often higher than posted limits.

Two additional raised crosswalks are scheduled for installation in front of Samoana High School and Marist Saint Francis School in Lepua.

Ta‘ase noted that construction had begun on a raised crosswalk in front of Laufou, but the department halted the project after extended traffic delays created significant congestion. Public Works has decided not to proceed with that location.

Ta‘ase told senators the project was publicly bid, and Paramount Construction was awarded the contract. He estimated the cost of each raised crosswalk at approximately $11,000.

Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean told the Public Works officials that in all his travels across the U.S. mainland, he has never seen road bumps like the ones recently installed. He questioned whether such structures were appropriate for primary roads and asked directly whether the raised crosswalks could be removed.

Deputy Director Ta‘ase confirmed that removal was possible. Tuaolo then advised that they be taken out to put an end to the steady stream of complaints from motorists and community members.

“It’s been nearly 50 years since American Samoa voted for their own governor,” he said. “The question that comes to mind is why now? Why wasn’t this done in all these years? This is very suspicious.”

Senator Magalei Logovii pressed Public Works officials on whether the Department of Public Safety (DPS) had been consulted before the raised crosswalks were installed. He noted that DPS typically provides assessments for any road project, including whether a proposed design might create a traffic hazard or pose risks to pedestrians and motorists.

Magalei repeatedly asked Ta‘ase whether the FHWA had formally approved the raised crosswalks. He requested written documentation from the federal agency confirming its authorization.

Senator Muagututi‘a Tauoa raised additional concerns, warning that the newly installed raised crosswalks could slow or obstruct emergency response vehicles, including EMS ambulances, police units, and the Fire Division. He said any roadway feature that delays emergency response times poses a serious public‑safety risk.

Muagututi‘a also questioned the cost of the installations, noting that at $11,000 per raised crosswalk, the price is “a lot of money” for a project that has already generated significant public frustration. He recommended leaving the three already constructed in place, but urged Public Works not to install any more until the Senate receives clearer justification and documentation from federal authorities.

He also recommended painting the raised crosswalks at Fatu‑ma‑Futi and Matafao to ensure drivers can clearly see them from a distance and recognize when they are approaching a pedestrian zone.

Muagututi‘a added that proper striping and visibility markings — similar to the treatment already applied to the raised crosswalk in front of Manumalo Academy — are essential for driver awareness and pedestrian safety. He said clear paint markings would help motorists recognize the crosswalks earlier and reduce confusion, especially given the complaints the installations have already generated.

Senator Ma‘o Faauma Gogo, however, sided with Senate President Tuaolo’s recommendation to remove the three raised crosswalks, arguing that traditional street‑sign warnings are sufficient to alert drivers to slow down near schools. He said clear signage has long been effective in school zones and questioned the need for additional roadway structures that have already caused confusion and frustration among motorists.

Ma’o also noted that teachers and students routinely assist with traffic control in front of their schools during morning drop‑off and afternoon pick‑up. He said this long‑standing practice has helped maintain safety without the need for raised crosswalks, and that the community’s involvement demonstrates that simpler, less disruptive measures can work.

Senator Leatualevao Asifoa, who requested the hearing with Public Works, said that based on the photos presented to lawmakers, there appeared to be very little difference between the raised crosswalks and traditional speed bumps. He questioned whether the installations met the design standards described by Public Works.

Senator Togiola T.A. Tulafono echoed those concerns, pointing out that the FHWA design photos showed raised crosswalks with a flat pedestrian surface, whereas the three already constructed in the Territory did not match that profile. He said the discrepancy raised questions about whether the installations were built to federal specifications.

Ta‘ase responded that additional work is planned to bring the crosswalks into compliance. He said the surfaces will be flattened to meet FHWA design requirements and will also be painted to improve visibility and pedestrian safety.

Editor’s Note: Samoa News notes that raised crosswalks are common in other countries, especially in school zones. They are clearly marked, sometimes with special lights (large yellow round bulbs) on each side of the walkway, with the walkway itself characteristically raised and flat, with the traditional stripes defining its width and length.

The ‘raised’ feature of the crosswalk is to make certain that a vehicle will slow down before proceeding.

Signage include those designating the speed limit as well as warning of approaching crosswalk, and are usually posted on both sides of the road as the raised crosswalk is approached.

There is also sometimes a small planted flower plot area on each side, enhancing the look of the raised crosswalk as a community beautification project.

Manumalo Academy student and teacher represent the territory at National History Day Young People’s Continental Congress

2026-08-07

By

Samoa News staff

reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Last month a local student and teacher pair —  Jaceyline Foketi Siliva and Ms. Grace Alesana from Manumalo Academy — represented American Samoa as one of 27 teams from across the US and the world to participate in the third annual Young People's Continental Congress, a joint program during National History Day (NHD).  The event appropriately took place in Philadelphia from July 19 to 25, at Carpenters’ Hall, the home of the nation’s First Continental Congress in 1774.

The Young People’s Continental Congress brought together 27 student-teacher teams from across the country in a study of America’s founding era and democratic ideals and to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. This year’s delegates represent diverse communities across the United States, including American Samoa, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and Department of Defense (DoDEA) schools in the Netherlands and Puerto Rico.

In preparation for the summer institute, student-teacher teams completed online learning modules throughout spring 2026 on the First Continental Congress and how our founding ideals evolved throughout U.S. history. Once in Philadelphia, teams experienced a week of special programming, including field learning opportunities at Carpenters’ Hall, Independence National Historical Park, the National Constitution Center, the Museum of the American Revolution, and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. During sessions with lead historians and museum professionals, students and teachers participated in discussions about how the ideals of the founding era have continued to be debated and refined over the last 250 years.

Delegates then co-created and signed a joint declaration of their aspirations for American democracy, just as their historical counterparts issued the Declaration of Colonial Rights and the Declaration of Independence.

“Programs like the Young People’s Continental Congress are fundamental to fostering intergenerational dialogue and much-needed discussions of democratic aspirations from diverse perspectives,” said NHD Executive Director, Dr. Cathy Gorn. “This fantastic group of students and teachers is a reminder of hope for the future, that the next generation is eager to learn about our revolutionary history, reflect on its legacy, and become thoughtful, engaged citizens in the process.”

“It’s so inspiring to watch our young delegates step up to embrace their role as citizens and find their voices,” said Carpenters’ Hall Executive Director, Michael Norris. “This Declaration of Aspirations is also a powerful way for us to remind policymakers and elected officials that young people care deeply about this country and want to be involved in strengthening our democracy.”

Congratulations to all the students and teacher teams who participated in the 2026 Young People’s Continental Congress.

Update: Manu’a residents meet to discuss Atu’u trust land

2026-08-06

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Many residents of Manu‘a are only now learning that they are collectively entitled to benefit from lease payments generated by businesses operating on the trust land in Atu‘u — property formally placed under a 1911 indenture by Paramount Chief Mauga Moimoi of Pago Pago.

In a meeting held last Friday the Manu‘a community discussed what steps they will need to take to make sure the oversight of the Atu‘u trust land and future lease payments are handled transparently and in accordance with the 1911 indenture.

The parcel of land in question is located directly across from Samoa Packing and it belongs to the Paramount Chief Mauga of Pago Pago. Records from the Registrar’s Office confirm that an indenture — a formal, legally binding agreement — was executed in 1911 by PC Mauga Moimoi, his wife Faapio, and then Manu‘a District Governor Tufele of Si‘ufaga, Manu‘a.

The indenture designates Tufele "as Trustee for the People of Manu‘a, (receipt whereof is hereby acknowledged) do by those presents grant, bargain, sell, convey and confirm unto the said party of the second part, as Trustee for the People of Manua, and to his successors and assigns forever, all that part or parcel of land situated in the village of Pago Pago, Tutuila, and known as the land Atu‘u… To have and to hold, all and singular, the above‑mentioned and described premises, together with the appurtenances, unto the said party of the second part, his successors or assigns IN TRUST, for the USE and BENEFIT of the People of Manu‘a.”

According to Land Commission Chairman Taesali Matagi, the indenture was originally executed by PC Mauga Moimoi to ensure that people from Manu‘a had land to reside on in Tutuila while working and supporting their families back home.

Over time, however, some Manu‘a residents who were assigned parcels under the trust arrangement began leasing those lands to foreign‑owned businesses and receiving monetary payments as lessors directly. This is a practice that continues to raise questions about who is the lessor and who is the lessee, and whether such private leasing aligns with the original intent of the 1911 trust agreement.

Taesali, who also serves as the Eastern District Governor’s representative on the Zoning Board, told Samoa News that the matter surfaced during a recent ZB meeting, where members reviewed several applications for commercial land lease variances bearing signatures of individuals other than the designated Trust Administrator. According to Taesali, board members questioned whether such private leasing aligns with the 1911 indenture that placed the land “in trust, for the use and benefit of the People of Manu‘a.”

The disclosure prompted board members to question how long private lease arrangements have been occurring, who authorized them, and whether the revenue has been flowing to the rightful beneficiaries under the trust.

Taesali said the permit review quickly evolved into a broader inquiry into the administration of trust land, leading to last Friday’s meeting where Manu‘a District Governor Poumele Apisa Galea'i, matai and residents scrutinized the implications of the indenture and the responsibilities of those occupying or managing parcels today.

Taesali, who convened the discussion, said the revelations surrounding private lease arrangements on trust land have prompted a wave of questions from residents who were never informed of their collective entitlement. The meeting, he noted, marked the first time many Manu‘a families had been formally briefed on the indenture’s terms and the trustee structure that governs the land today.

“Several people thanked me for raising this important issue and enlightening them about their entitlement,” he revealed, noting that many did not know the specific terms of the 1911 indenture or the communal rights it established. “They told me they were completely unaware of the trust language and what it meant for them as beneficiaries.”

He added that the lack of awareness may not have been accidental. “I suspect the people who were benefitting from lease payments knew,” he said, “but didn’t want to disclose those details. Others may have known but didn't want to rock the boat because of family ties, or they were receiving some sort of compensation on the side.”

Taesali noted that it has now been 115 years since the indenture — a formal, legally binding agreement — was executed in 1911 and established a communal ownership structure intended to protect Manu‘a families working and residing in Tutuila.

Yet despite the clarity of the trust language, Taesali said the leasing of Atu‘u trust land to foreign businesses began in the 1970s, creating a half‑century pattern in which individuals — not the Manu‘a community as a whole — received lease payments.

“That’s fifty years of people benefiting privately from land that was supposed to be held in trust for everyone in Manu‘a,” he said, adding that the long‑standing practice has diverted revenue away from the beneficiaries the indenture was designed to protect.

The timeline, he emphasized, shows how far the administration of the trust has drifted from its original intent, and why a full review of the trust’s management is now urgently needed.

Taesali told participants at last Friday’s meeting that the Manu‘a community must take immediate steps to reclaim oversight of the Atu‘u trust land and ensure that future lease payments are handled transparently and in accordance with the 1911 indenture.

He advised the group to establish a committee dedicated to monitoring and managing a trust fund sourced from Atu‘u lease revenues. The committee, he said, should include representatives from every Manu‘a village and be chaired by the Manu‘a District Governor, who would serve as the Trustee — or Lessor — of the Atu‘u trust land.

Taesali explained that this structure is both practical and historically consistent, noting that the Tufele title has remained vacant since the passing of Tufele Li‘amatua Tufele, leaving the District Governor as the most appropriate figure to assume trustee responsibilities under the indenture.

Taesali said he also urged the group to retain an attorney to handle the legal aspects of reorganizing the trust’s administration. He reminded attendees that Manu‘a has sons and daughters who are certified lawyers and suggested former Lt. Governor La‘apui E.V. Ale, who is also a matai from Manu‘a. His recommendation, however, was met with resistance. Former Police Commissioner Ta‘aga Saite Moliga objected, arguing that La‘apui was currently at odds with their village council and was not officially recognized.

Taesali said he clarified the matter by reminding the group that the Atu‘u trust land does not belong to any single village — it belongs to all the people of Manu‘a. “This is not a village issue,” he told them. “This is a Manu‘a issue.”

(Of note, La‘apui arrived at the meeting only moments later — just as the discussion had shifted to the second major issue under scrutiny that morning: the potential impacts of deep‑sea mining on the islands and residents of Manu‘a.)

Regarding the Atu‘u land trust, Taesali reiterated that the issue is fundamentally a moral failure — one that has persisted for decades because no one was willing to confront it or expose what was happening. He said that during a recent Zoning Board review of an application to renew a commercial land‑lease variance, one of the applicants disclosed that the current lease rate was $3,000 a month.

“That’s $36,000 a year,” Taesali calculated. “And this has been going on for decades. It is clear the people of Manu‘a are missing out on a significant amount of money owed to them because of selfish individuals who are pocketing funds that do not belong to them, and spineless people who refuse to speak up because of personal connections.”

Taesali said that as a member of the Zoning Board, he will formally advise the board in writing to defer any decision on the commercial land‑leasing application involving the Atu‘u trust land until the matter is properly reviewed and the trust’s beneficiaries are protected.

Taesali, whose father is from Faleasao, said the issue carries personal weight for him. He told Samoa News that the people of Manu‘a have been denied benefits they are rightfully entitled to for far too long, and he intends to “do the right thing” by ensuring the trust is finally administered as intended.

“This land was set aside for our people,” he said, “and the benefits were meant to support all of Manu‘a, not just a few individuals.”

Manu‘a District Governor Poumele Apisa Galea‘i echoed Taesali’s sentiments, stressing that the Atu‘u trust arrangement is not simply a historical artifact but a legally binding agreement that continues to dictate how the land must be administered today.

Poumele announced that the issue will be formally discussed — with hopes of reaching a consensus on the next plan of action — at a meeting scheduled for August 14, 2026.

He said the upcoming session will bring Manu‘a leadership together to determine how the Atu‘u trust should be administered moving forward and how lease revenues should be safeguarded for the rightful beneficiaries.

BACKGROUND

Samoa News should point out that a court case in 1988, concerning the scope of the authority vested in the Trustee as per the 1911 Warranty Deed, made several key findings:

1 — The deed from Mauga Moimoi to “Tufele and his successors or assigns” created a valid trust for the use and benefit of the people of Manu‘a; and,

2 — Trusteeship follows the matai title — The trusteeship automatically devolves to each successive holder of the Tufele matai title, not to the heirs or estate of any individual titleholder.

As noted, the Tufele title has remained vacant since the passing of Tufele Li‘amatua Tufele. Whether the Atu’u trusteeship can now be assigned to another ‘authority’ is in question.

Port Admin & Samoa Airways Launch Response & Recovery Operation of Aircraft Incident in Fitiuta

2026-08-05

By

LALI STAFF

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Port Administration American Samoa (PAAS) and Samoa Airways officials have launched a coordinated response and recovery operation following a runway deviation incident that occurred at Fitiuta Airport, Manu’a Islands on Tuesday, July 28, 2026.

No fatalities or major injuries were reported. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) was promptly notified, conducted its initial review, and has officially released the aircraft back to the operator for recovery.

IMMEDIATE AIRPORT RESPONSE AND INVESTIGATION

Under the direction of PAAS Airport Manager Tevita Fuimono and PAAS Deputy Director Tumua Matu'u, airport operations immediately secured the site and initiated a factual investigation. The airport's scope is strictly focused on operational response times, personnel deployment, and runway conditions. A preliminary visual inspection of the 3,200-foot runway showed no cracks or obstacles at the deviation site.

Airport personnel have documented the scene using drone video and photographic evidence, capturing approximately 26 official records of tire tracks and the aircraft's final position. Preliminary track analysis indicates the aircraft's nose and main gears touched down before the nose track gradually deviated to the right. Airport officials emphasized that they will present only factual data and will avoid attributing a cause to the incident, leaving the final determination to transport safety authorities and Samoa Airways.

PRELIMINARY AIRCRAFT CONDITION

Initial exterior observations handled by the airport team noted the following:

1.  Nose Gear: Collapsed, with a minor visible gap in the nose section indicating potential structural concerns.

2.  Left Landing Gear: Tire is flat, and the gear is currently wedged in nearby brush.

3.  Propeller: Dented, consistent with contact with vegetation.

4.  Wings and Belly: No obvious exterior wing damage was visible; the underbelly and left wing edge conditions remain unconfirmed.

AIRCRAFT RECOVERY AND LOGISTICS PLAN

After a video conference call on Monday, August 3, 2026, with PAAS, Samoa Airways CEO Fauo'o Fatu Tielu is finalizing a recovery strategy in partnership with Unity Aviation of Canada, which is preparing to deploy a specialized 2–3 person rescue team. The airline is also engaging local civil engineering resources to secure cranes and forklifts.

The recovery will follow a strict sequential process:

1.  Relocation: Lift and move the aircraft from the brush to a designated staging corner on the airport apron.

2.  Inspection: Conduct a thorough structural assessment.

3.  Disposal/Transport: If the aircraft is deemed repairable, it will be prepared for a ferry flight. If it cannot be safely flown, it will be carefully dismantled on-site and shipped via two 40-foot cargo containers.

The recovery efforts to eventually move (fly or ship) the aircraft to Apia, Samoa may take at least 2-3 months.

SAFETY, STAGING, AND SITE COORDINATION

To protect the airfield infrastructure, PAAS Engineering Manager Natalia Palamo will oversee the aircraft's physical relocation. The airline must submit a comprehensive recovery plan—including timing, heavy equipment loads, and crane weights—prior to moving the aircraft to ensure the protection of airport pavements and airfield lighting.

The airport has cleared apron space for the aircraft and will permit a securely bolted temporary tent to shield the team from high winds during the operation. To maintain strict airfield security and prevent unauthorized access, Samoa Airways will provide a verified list of authorized personnel before they enter the site.

NEXT STEPS

PAAS has established a shared digital repository to transparently provide the airline with all official drone footage, track measurements, and the forthcoming written investigation summary. Samoa Airways technical representatives are scheduled to conduct an immediate post-meeting physical assessment of the aircraft to finalize equipment and staging requirements.

Do you still have Crown Lynn memories in your house?

2026-07-31

Source: RNZ Pacific

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — In the 1970’s, a small retail store — Ho-Ching Annesley, Inc. — in American Samoa — sold foodstuffs, but was well-known locally for selling affordable plates, bowls, cups & saucers. The Crown Lynn pottery was brought in by the company from New Zealand, in a container over the following years, as ‘seconds’ — meaning they did not make the mark to be sold by Crown Lynn Potteries, Ltd. due to a variety of imperfections during kiln firing. However, they were sold by as miscellaneous sales; and, they found a perfect market in American Samoa at the time.

When a container came in, the word would go out, and crowds of women of all ages would be seen sitting in front of the shelves that held the pottery, on the floor, cross-legged — hand sorting, mix matching their choices for their household plates, bowls, cups & saucers.

At the time of the Crown Lynn factory’s closure, a third of the workforce was from Samoa, according to the Te Toi Aku - Crown Lynn & Clay Museum that reopened the last brickworks kiln in Auckland, NZ recently, with a display space for ceramic and pottery artists.

The museum’s director Louise Stevenson told Culture 101/ RNZ- Life and Culture, that each handle and rim of Crown Lynn cups looks slightly different. “It makes you think about the fact that every single crown and cup that was made, we’ve identified, would have had 14 pairs of hands involved in the process of making.”

For American Samoa, Samoa News notes to this day, some local households still have remnants of their mother’s or grandmother’s collection of dishes that are pieces that hold memories of eating meals, and sharing food with your family and friends. [photo: RNZ/ Braydon Priest]

First American Samoa resident earns UH online social work degree

2026-07-31

By

University of Hawaii News

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — When Vivian Legaloimoe Ho Ching was named first runner-up in the 2026 Miss American Samoa contest, she added another remarkable achievement to a journey already defined by service, leadership and dedication to her community.

A recent graduate of the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s Thompson School of Social Work & Public Health, Ho Ching is the first student to complete the Master of Social Work (MSW) online program while residing in American Samoa. Her accomplishment highlights the importance of creating pathways that allow students to pursue advanced degrees while remaining in their home communities.

“Vivian represents the very best of what is possible when educational opportunity, cultural identity and community service come together,” said Theresa Kreif, director of Pacific Partnerships and Workforce Development Initiatives. “Her success demonstrates that students can pursue advanced education while remaining connected to their families and cultural values.”

“Increasing access to our online social work programs allows students throughout the Pacific to pursue a high-quality education without having to leave the communities they plan to serve,” said Meripa Godinet, associate dean of the Thompson School. “Vivian’s achievement demonstrates how accessible educational pathways can prepare local professionals, strengthen the regional social service workforce, and create lasting benefits for families and communities. Her accomplishment also honors the social work alumni connected to American Samoa who came before her, whose service, leadership, and commitment helped establish a strong foundation for future generations of social workers.”

A COMMITMENT TO SERVICE

For Ho Ching, both her education and her pageant role are grounded in a commitment to service. While completing her MSW field internship at the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs clinic in American Samoa, she provided support to veterans and their families, developing skills grounded in Pacific values.

“My journey has always been about giving back to the community that has shaped me,” said Ho Ching. “Earning my MSW while remaining in American Samoa allowed me to stay connected to my culture and grow as a professional.”

As first runner-up in the Miss American Samoa contest, Ho Ching serves as a cultural ambassador, advocating for issues important to Pacific communities. Her social work background reinforces this role, emphasizing advocacy, social justice, and community wellbeing.

“I see both social work and the pageant experience as opportunities to uplift others,” she said. “Both are rooted in listening to people and working to create positive change.”

Ho Ching’s success reflects the Thompson School’s broader commitment to strengthening the social service workforce throughout the Pacific. Her achievement serves as a model for future students, proving that advanced education can be pursued without leaving home, while bridging the gap between professional expertise and cultural stewardship.

UPDATE: Aircraft incident at Fitiuta Airport

2026-07-30

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Port Administration American Samoa (PAAS) is providing an update regarding the runway excursion on Tuesday, July 28, 2026 involving Samoa Airways Twin Otter (5W-FAY) Flight 990, at Fitiuta Airport, Manu’a Islands.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has completed its initial assessment and has officially released the aircraft from its investigative hold. PAAS will continue its investigation of the runway excursion today and tomorrow. PAAS will also coordinate with Samoa Airways on the next steps for the removal and recovery of the aircraft.

The runway is open with normal flight operations, with two Samoa Airways flights operating today. A Samoa Airways engineer is now onsite. The flight advisory remains in effect while recovery operations are coordinated.

As previously announced, due to the unavailability of a chartered aircraft today, PAAS has arranged for a charter flight today — Thursday July 30th — to continue its onsite investigation. Port Director Barney Sene and members of the Airport investigation team will travel to Fitiuta to assess the incident site, coordinate recovery operations with Samoa Airways, and the safe restoration of the affected area.

The aircraft and the immediate surrounding area continue to be secured by PAAS while recovery plans are finalized.

PAAS appreciates the continued support and cooperation of all partner agencies involved in the response. Additional information will be released as it becomes available.

Lewis Wolman: Nov 20, 1957 — Jul 25, 2026

2026-07-29

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Lewis Joel Wolman passed away peacefully at home in Boulder, Colorado, on Saturday, July 25, 2026, with his family by his side.

Lewis was born November 20, 1957, in Madison, Wisconsin, to Joseph "Murphy" Martin Wolman and Anne Wolman. The youngest of 5 siblings, he grew up around the newspaper business, which instilled a curiosity and passion for the news, public issues, reading, community, service, and lifting people and places.

He graduated from West High School in Madison in 1974 at 17 years old. After one year of school at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, he headed out west to the University of California, Santa Cruz, where he graduated with a degree in Environmental Planning.

He eventually got a job as a Program Officer in the U.S. Office of Coastal Management, which took him to American Samoa, where he would spend the better part of the next 40 years.

In American Samoa, he built a wonderful life and career. He met his wife, Eletise Matagi, raised four children (Tavie, Jessica, Homer, Iopa), and held many leadership positions in both the private and public sectors.

He was perhaps most recognizable for his work as the publisher and editor of the Samoa News for 20 years, where he worked tirelessly to keep the people informed of the issues that mattered most to the people of American Samoa.

His career after Samoa News included, but was not limited to, Country Manager of Bluesky Communications, CEO of ASTCA, President of the American Samoa Chamber of Commerce, CEO of the GHC Reid Group, and Special Advisor to the Governor of American Samoa. He loved to work.

While his work kept him busy, Lewis still made his family a priority. He took the time to listen, ask thoughtful questions, got to know you on a deeper level, and found quiet ways to show you he cared.

He loved a good bike ride, walk, traveling, tennis, the arts, funky dancing, and was a voracious reader and writer.

Samoa News management and staff send love and condolences to his wife, Eletise Matagi Wolman; children: Tavie, Jessica, Homer, Iopa; and his sisters Nicky and Ruth; and his 14 grandchildren: Emelia, Ma'ata, Lewy, Fatu, Eden, AJ, Tali, Tunoa, Sina, Vao, Fin, Moana, Murphy, Talia; and many nieces and nephews.

His celebration of life will be held on Tuesday, August 4, 2026, at the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints meetinghouse on 4655 Table Mesa Dr., Boulder, CO.

via US Navy Institute

Economic development a key priority for Administration

2026-07-28

By

Samoa News staff

reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Governor Pulaalii Nikolao Pula noted that the proposed budget for Fiscal Year 2027 reflects an Administration focusing on building a stronger, more resilient, and self-sustaining economy rather than just achieving immediate fiscal stabilization. He acknowledged that while challenges persist, the progress made over the last two fiscal years lays a solid foundation for continued growth and responsible governance.

As reported earlier by Samoa News, the proposed budget totals $789.3 million, representing a 2 percent decrease from the FY 2026 budget.

Samoa News notes that two points should be acknowledged about the FY 2027 budget submission. First, the governor’s ceiling set forth in his call letter was for $133 million, while the budget documents are now reporting $137.9 million; and, second, it’s unknown if either ceiling amounts account for the government’s debt service or other pledged revenues — these are amounts that ASG are obligated pay before government operations are funded.

The Governor emphasized that American Samoa's long-term success relies on maintaining sound fiscal discipline and making strategic investments aimed at strengthening the economy, modernizing government operations, and enhancing the quality of life for residents. He points out that federal pandemic assistance programs are winding down, making the Territory increasingly depend more on sustainable local revenues, prudent financial management, and policies that foster private-sector investment and economic diversification.

The Pula and Pulu Administration says that it is committed to ensuring structurally balanced budgets, which are supported by realistic revenue projections and responsible spending controls, which safeguards essential public services while safeguarding the Territory's long-term financial health and minimizing reliance on one-time funding sources.

At the heart of its efforts is economic development — a key priority for the Administration. As such, the governor says it is focusing on investments in critical infrastructure — such as transportation, ports, broadband connectivity, energy resilience, water systems, healthcare facilities, and public safety — looking to create new commercial opportunities, enhance government services, and boost American Samoa's competitiveness within the Pacific region.

The Administration is touting several transformational initiatives that it believes are poised to positively impact the Territory’s economic outlook. They are:

The Google Le Vasa submarine cable project, once completed, will significantly enhance broadband capacity and improve digital connectivity for businesses, educational institutions, healthcare providers, and government entities.

The implementation of the Port Development Vision that aims to modernize maritime infrastructure, enhance regional trade, boost cargo efficiency, and position Pago Pago Harbor as a more competitive logistics hub in the Pacific.

The Administration states that it also recognizes that long-term prosperity hinges on strengthening the Territory’s workforce. As such, investments in education, vocational training, healthcare recruitment and retention, as well as workforce development programs, will continue to prepare American Samoa’s residents for emerging job opportunities while decreasing reliance on imported labor in critical sectors.

Enhancing government efficiency is another vital goal, the Administration is promoting — especially in how it handles its money. Ongoing modernization of financial management systems, tax administration, procurement processes, customs operations, and digital government services, it says will improve transparency, enhance accountability, boost revenue collection, and provide improved public services while gradually reducing administrative costs.

It is also addressing its longstanding financial obligations. The Administration states that it is committed to collaborating with stakeholders to strengthen the Government Employees' Retirement Fund, responsibly manage government liabilities, and enhance the Territory's long-term financial standing without compromising current public services.

Continuing, the Administration acknowledges that federal partnerships will remain crucial for American Samoa’s future. The Administration says it will actively pursue competitive federal grants, infrastructure funding opportunities, and strategic partnerships that leverage local investments. It will also advocate for equitable federal policies that address the unique geographic and economic challenges facing America's southernmost territory.

Despite uncertainties stemming from global economic conditions, inflationary pressures, fuel prices, supply chain disruptions, and geopolitical developments, the Administration says that American Samoa enters Fiscal Year 2027 from a position of improved fiscal stability compared to recent years. This is a result of conservative budgeting, disciplined financial management, and continued economic development investments that have fortified the Territory's capability to tackle future challenges while seizing emerging opportunities.

The governor characterized the Fiscal Year 2027 Budget as transcending mere annual financial planning; it embodies a long-term pledge to responsible governance, economic resilience, and sustainable growth.

For the upcoming budget review, the governor states that the Administration remains devoted to collaborating with the Fono, the Judiciary, federal partners, village leaders, and the residents of American Samoa. Though differences in perspective are natural within a representative governance framework, the shared responsibility to enhance the quality of life for those we serve remains unchanged.

Senate unanimously confirms Roy J.D. Hall Jr. as Administrative Law Judge

2026-07-28

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Roy J.D. Hall, Jr., one of American Samoa’s most senior attorneys, was unanimously confirmed yesterday to serve as the Territory’s Administrative Law Judge. All 17 senators present for the Senate vote supported his appointment, reflecting broad legislative confidence in his legal experience and long service to the community.

Hall becomes the fourth person to hold the position, which oversees administrative hearings, adjudicates regulatory disputes, and ensures due‑process protections across government agencies.

During his confirmation hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee, chaired by Senator Leatuaolevao Asifoa, veteran attorney Roy J.D. Hall Jr. delivered a reflective and heartfelt summary of his 52 years in the legal profession — a career spanning private practice, government service, legislative counsel, and judicial roles. Hall said he was grateful for “another opportunity to serve the people and government of American Samoa.”

He thanked Governor Pulaali‘i Nikolao Pula for nominating him and opened his remarks by praising God for sustaining him throughout his decades of service.

Hall devoted a portion of his testimony to acknowledging the people who shaped his life and career. He paid tribute to his late parents — Roy J.D. Hall Sr., a retired U.S. Navy veteran from Pago Pago, and Toaiva Ofoia of Vaitogi — crediting them for instilling in him a strong Christian faith, respect for elders, and pride in his Samoan heritage.

He also recognized the support of his siblings, recalling their encouragement during his childhood health challenges and later educational pursuits. Hall thanked his wife Jacklyn and their children for standing by him through “the long days and hours” of private practice and his years as Deputy Attorney General. Their love, he said, gave him the strength to pursue his lifelong dream of becoming an attorney.

Hall’s résumé reflects one of the most extensive public‑service records in the Territory. He served two terms in the House of Representatives, worked as a District Court Judge Pro Tempore, chaired both the American Samoa Visitors Bureau and the Board of Directors of ASTCA, and provided legal counsel to the Senate under then‑President Lolo Letalu Moliga.

He also served as counsel to the Senate Select Investigative Committee (SSIC) and has spent the last four years as Deputy Attorney General, handling complex legal matters on behalf of the government.

In the Senate chamber, Hall pledged that if confirmed, his rulings would be grounded in fairness, integrity, and respect for constitutional rights.

“My goal as an attorney was to ensure that all parties receive their constitutional right to due process and a fair and impartial trial,” Hall said. “If confirmed to serve as Administrative Law Judge, I will apply these same principles of fairness, integrity, constitutional and judicial due process to everyone who comes before the Administrative Law Court.”

Committee Chair Leatuaolevao noted that senators were well aware of Hall’s long service and said his credentials were unquestioned. Leatuaolevao briefly asked Hall for his opinion on the unsettled issue of director confirmations, referencing the Fono’s position that all directors should be submitted for confirmation versus the Governor’s stance that directors of line agencies under his office need not be confirmed. After posing the question, Leatuaolevao added that Hall did not need to answer.

Senator Gaoteote Palaie Tofau also spoke highly of Hall’s experience and expressed full support for his nomination. Gaoteote noted that some directors appear at hearings represented by attorneys, and asked Hall why this occurs. Hall explained that while confirmation hearings do not require legal counsel, a subpoena does, and in those cases the Attorney General’s Office appears with the witness.

Senator Muagututi‘a Tauoa said he had no doubts about Hall’s qualifications but offered fatherly advice. As a son of Samoa, he said, Hall should be able to address district leaders in Samoan when appearing before the Senate. He also urged Hall to be fair, treat everyone equally, and avoid discrimination.

Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean remarked that Hall and former Governor Togiola T.A. Tulafono are now the Territory’s most senior attorneys. He revealed that the Senate had been considering Hall for the role of Senate Legal Counsel, following the departure of Senate Attorney Mitzie Jessop‑Ta‘afua to the Retirement Fund Office. Tuaolo joked that perhaps the Governor, hearing of those plans, moved quickly to appoint Hall as Administrative Law Judge.

Tuaolo acknowledged Senator Muagututi‘a’s advice about speaking Samoan, noting that Hall may find English more natural in legal settings because it is the language of the courts.

Hall succeeds Marie Alailima, who has served as Administrative Law Judge since 2007.
